description: Site header with logo, primary navigation menu, and hamburger toggle on mobile. Reads a registered WP nav menu by theme location. Template-owned chrome (issue 223): it is rendered once by the theme, never composed. It is styled through the `nav` entry of the pp_site_udc site option (update_site_option) using the roles below — the same engine, grammar, groups, @token references, breakpoints, :hover/:focus-visible/:active state maps and presets a band's `udc` takes. It declares ZERO style props and zero style slots; the props below are content and configuration only. STATES ARE DEFAULTS NOW (#994, fixing #992): every role below carries the header's resting appearance AND its interaction treatment as role defaults, so setting `typography.color` at REST no longer cancels that role's hover or the current-page marker — they sit in the same unlayered tier your value does and win on specificity. Setting a `":hover"` map is an override, not a rescue. TWO THINGS STILL NEED YOU: set `submenu-toggle` whenever you set `link`, because the dropdown chevron is the link's SIBLING and nothing can make it follow the link colour on its own (#995); and remember a `"_preset"` fills in only where a role's defaults are SILENT, because role defaults out-rank presets.

location.description: WP theme location slug for the nav menu.

logo_text.description: Logo text wordmark. Falls back to pp_site_title() when empty. Shown when no logo image resolves. TEMPLATE CONTRACT (issue 582): NOT reachable from any supported surface — base.php never passes it and a page cannot compose a nav, so it always resolves to the site title in practice. It is documented here because pp_resolve_logo() accepts it, not because you can set it. To change the wordmark, change the site title.
logo_text.conditionality_note: NO logo image resolves — a negation the grammar cannot express; with a valid logo_id the image wins and this wordmark is never rendered

logo_id.description: Media Library attachment ID for the logo image (NOT a URL). When set to a valid image it renders an img tag instead of the text wordmark. Resolution order: this prop, then the pp_logo_id site option, then the WP custom_logo theme-mod. TEMPLATE CONTRACT (issue 582): NOT reachable as a prop — base.php never passes it and a composition naming nav is rejected outright with template_owned_component, so the prop-level image check can never actually run on it. Set the logo through the pp_logo_id SITE OPTION (update_site_option); that is the write the image-attachment rule validates — a non-image or non-existent ID is rejected there.

logo_alt.description: Alt text for the logo image. Defaults to the attachment's own alt metadata, then logo_text/site title; it is never empty. TEMPLATE CONTRACT (issue 582): template-supplied, not page-authored — base.php maps the pp_logo_alt SITE OPTION onto this prop, so update_site_option with key pp_logo_alt is the surface. Use it only when the alt should differ from the attachment's own alt metadata; leave it unset otherwise and the attachment's alt is used. The same option also feeds the footer logo. A value that is empty OR WHITESPACE-ONLY counts as unprovided and falls through to the rest of the chain rather than rendering — a blank alt would announce nothing and would suppress the attachment's own alt. A real value renders verbatim, surrounding spaces included.
logo_alt.conditionality_note: a logo IMAGE resolves, i.e. logo_id points at a real image attachment — a numeric-prop precondition the grammar, whose `present` predicate covers strings and arrays only, cannot express

_band.description: The <header class="site-header"> itself — the whole header bar. Set the site header's background and border here.

container.description: The header ROW: the flex line holding the logo, the hamburger and the menu. Set the row's height with sizing.min-height and the space between its items with spacing.gap — those two are why this role exists. This is the row, not the bar: the bar's own background and border are the _band role, so a background here paints an inset band inside the header rather than the header itself. Typography set here only reaches text that does not set its own colour, and every text element in the row (logo, links, the toggle) has its own role — so set colour on those roles, not on this one.

logo.description: The logo link: the wordmark when no logo image resolves, and the link wrapping the image when one does. Its accent hover is a role default, so setting `typography.color` here keeps the hover; set a `":hover"` colour to override it. The 44px `sizing.min-height` is a pointer-target floor, the same one `.nav__toggle`'s 44x44 keeps structurally — lower it only deliberately.

logo-image.description: The logo , when a logo image attachment resolves. Size it here.

menu.description: The menu container. On phones this is the disclosure panel the hamburger opens, so its background is what a mobile visitor sees behind the links. Its phone-only shadow is a bespoke elevation (`0 8px 24px rgba(16, 24, 40, 0.12)`), shared with the `submenu` dropdown so the two panels read as one surface family; none of the theme's `--shadow-*` tokens matches it, which is why it is written out rather than referenced.

obligations.why: `link` declares its own colour and accent hover, so a colour set here never reaches the menu links. Set `link` and its `:hover`.
`link-current` declares its own accent colour for the you-are-here marker, so a colour set here never reaches it.

menu-list.description: The menu LIST itself (the <ul> WordPress emits, and any nested one). Its `spacing.gap` is the space between menu items in both directions — the mobile stack and the desktop row share one value. This is the list, not the panel: the panel's background and padding are the `menu` role, and the desktop dropdown panel is `submenu`.

obligations.why: `link` declares its own colour and accent hover, so a colour set here never reaches the menu links. Set `link` and its `:hover`.
`link-current` declares its own accent colour for the you-are-here marker, so a colour set here never reaches it.

submenu.description: The desktop dropdown panel for a menu item that has children. It is a separate surface from `menu`: the mobile disclosure panel and the desktop dropdown used to share one colour knob and fall back differently, which is exactly the hidden coupling that made the old surface hard to reason about. Its shadow is the same bespoke elevation the mobile `menu` panel uses, deliberately: the two are the same kind of floating surface at different widths.

submenu-toggle.description: The dropdown disclosure button beside a menu item that has children — the chevron. SET THIS WHENEVER YOU SET `link`: the button is a SIBLING of the link, not a child, so it cannot follow the link's colour on its own, and a header styled dark without it leaves the chevron on the default ink against your new background, invisible (#995). It is rendered only where a menu item actually has children, and it is hidden until JavaScript activates the disclosure.

link.description: Every nav link at rest. Its accent hover is a role default and the you-are-here marker is the `link-current` role's, so setting `typography.color` here cancels neither (#992 was fixed by #994). Use the :hover, :focus-visible and :active states here to OVERRIDE the built-in interaction treatment rather than to restore it.

obligations.why: `link-current` adds a compound to the same <a> and defaults to the accent, so it beats a colour set here on the current page. Set both.

link-current.description: The link for the page the visitor is on. WordPress marks it current-menu-item on every item it considers current — that class is a superset of current_page_item and of aria-current="page", which core only ever sets alongside it — so this one selector reaches them all. It targets that item's own link as a DIRECT CHILD, so a current page that has a dropdown does not hand the treatment to every link inside it. Both its accent colour and its bold weight are defaults of this role; set values here to change them.

toggle.description: The hamburger button, shown on phones only. Its two icons are swapped by structural CSS, not by anything set here, and they inherit this role's colour. Its accent hover is a role default, so setting `typography.color` here keeps it; set a `":hover"` colour to override.
